sourceTitleEnglish: Tell a daily routine in order
sourceObjectiveEnglish: Tell a daily routine in order: A reflexive pronoun changes with the person: me, te, se, nos, se.
sourceFocusEnglish: Tell a daily routine in order
sourceSpeakingEnglish: Role-play La mañana de Julia with a patient classmate. Practice tell a daily routine in order. Use this lesson's grammar, ask a related question, answer the partner, and confirm understanding. Keep language at beginner level; explain unfamiliar words in English when asked.

sourceGrammarEnglish.focus: A reflexive pronoun changes with the person: me, te, se, nos, se. In me levanto, the person getting up is also the subject. Put the pronoun before a conjugated verb.

examples.es: Julia se despierta a las seis.
Se levanta y abre la ventana.
examples.en: She gets up and opens the window.

cards.decisionNote: Spanish me groups object and reflexive senses. French me/m' needs verb and pronoun role context.
Spanish te groups object and reflexive senses. French te/t' also requires register and verb context.
Source clase groups class and classroom; French cours/classe/salle de classe are context-specific.
Source la groups feminine article and object/person pronouns; French la/l' needs grammatical role and elision context.
Spanish las marks feminine plural article/object; French les does not preserve that gender contrast.
Source para groups for and purpose; French pour requires an object or infinitive context.
Source de groups of and from; French de needs phrase-level sense and contractions.
Source por groups through and because of; the nighttime phrase is temporal, not either isolated glossary sense.

archivedRedesign.title: Raconter une habitude et son interruption
archivedRedesign.scene: Une équipe prépare une présentation comme d’habitude, mais le projecteur cesse de fonctionner avant la répétition.
archivedRedesign.reason: The archived interrupted-projector rehearsal teaches past routine and interruption; the current source is a simple reflexive morning routine.

sourceDecisions: The pinned Spanish objective teaches me/te/se/nos/se before a conjugated reflexive verb; French me/te/se/nous/se has elision and person-specific morphology, so write a French objective instead of translating the Spanish paradigm mechanically.
The current source places a beginner morning-routine/reflexive-pronoun lesson at Master 14; qualified curriculum review must decide placement without changing saved identity silently.
Grouped article, pronoun, class/classroom and preposition faces require contextual dictionary senses; Spanish feminine plural las does not map to a French gender distinction in les.
The source's te question is informal singular. French tu is conditional pending a speaking-role/register decision.
